los.text: Describe the major diseases and risk factors for ill health at the global level and how they are measured
los.html:
Global burden of disease (GBD)
  • Leading causes of death worldwide are ischaemic heart disease, stroke, COPD, lower respiratory infections, neonatal conditions
  • Lung cancer
  • Diabetes
  • CKD
  • Diarrhoeal disease
  • TB (COVID-19 transiently).
  • Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) cause ~70%+ of deaths, now including in LMICs ("epidemiological transition" and double burden: infections + NCDs).
Leading risk factors
  • High blood pressure (top)
  • Tobacco
  • Air pollution (household and ambient)
  • High fasting glucose
  • High BMI
  • Poor diet
  • Child and maternal malnutrition
  • Alcohol
  • Unsafe water/sanitation/hygiene (WASH)
  • High LDL.
Measurement
  • Mortality: crude and age-standardised death rates, life expectancy, infant mortality rate (per 1,000 live births), under-5 mortality rate, maternal mortality ratio (per 100,000 live births).
  • DALYs (disability-adjusted life years) = YLL (years of life lost) + YLD (years lived with disability); one DALY = one lost year of healthy life. Used by GBD/WHO to compare burden across diseases.
  • QALYs (cost-effectiveness), HALE (health-adjusted life expectancy).
  • Data sources: vital registration (often incomplete in LMICs), Demographic and Health Surveys, verbal autopsy, disease surveillance, censuses, modelling (IHME).
DeterminantsPoverty, education (especially of women), gender inequality, conflict, climate change, urbanisation, health-system strength.

los.text: Describe the major causes of global childhood morbidity and mortality (compare with UK).
sessions: Sustainable Development Goals: global health for future generations
los.html:
Global under-5 deaths~5 million/year (fallen >50% since 1990); ~half in the neonatal period; most in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.
Main causes
  • Neonatal conditions (preterm birth complications, birth asphyxia/trauma, neonatal sepsis, congenital anomalies), pneumonia (leading infectious killer), diarrhoea, malaria, measles, HIV, injuries.
  • Undernutrition underlies ~45% of child deaths.
MorbidityStunting (chronic malnutrition, ~150 million children), anaemia, malaria, worms, developmental delay.
SDG 3.2End preventable deaths of newborns and under-5s by 2030: neonatal mortality ≤12 and under-5 mortality ≤25 per 1,000 live births.
UK comparison
  • Under-5 mortality ~4 per 1,000 (vs >70 in some sub-Saharan countries).
  • UK causes: prematurity/low birthweight, congenital anomalies, SIDS, injuries, cancer
  • Infections rarely.
  • UK has higher infant mortality than many western European countries, with a strong deprivation gradient and higher rates in some ethnic minority groups.
Interventions
  • Skilled birth attendance
  • Neonatal resuscitation
  • Kangaroo care
  • Exclusive breastfeeding
  • Vaccines (pneumococcal, rotavirus, measles, Hib)
  • ORS + zinc
  • Antibiotics for pneumonia (amoxicillin)
  • Insecticide-treated bed nets
  • Vitamin A
  • WASH
  • IMCI (Integrated Management of Childhood Illness).

los.text: Describe the causes, prevention and treatment of childhood malnutrition and diarrhoeal diseases in the developing world
los.html:
Malnutrition
  • Undernutrition (wasting, stunting, underweight, micronutrient deficiency) and overnutrition.
  • Wasting (acute; weight-for-height < −2 SD); severe acute malnutrition (SAM): WHZ < −3, MUAC <115 mm, or bilateral pitting oedema (kwashiorkor: oedema, skin/hair changes, fatty liver; marasmus: severe wasting).
  • Stunting (chronic; height-for-age < −2 SD): irreversible after ~2 years ("first 1,000 days").
Causes
  • Poverty
  • Food insecurity
  • Poor maternal nutrition/LBW
  • Short or no breastfeeding
  • Poor complementary feeding
  • Recurrent infections (diarrhoea, measles, HIV, TB, worms) → vicious cycle of infection and malnutrition
  • Poor WASH
  • Conflict
  • Climate.
DiarrhoeaRotavirus, Cryptosporidium, Shigella, ETEC, cholera. Kills via dehydration; persistent diarrhoea worsens malnutrition.
Treatment
  • Diarrhoea: low-osmolarity ORS (glucose–sodium co-transport), zinc for 10–14 days (↓ duration and recurrence), continue feeding/breastfeeding; IV fluids for severe dehydration; antibiotics only for dysentery/cholera.
  • SAM: uncomplicated → community-based ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF); complicated → inpatient (WHO 10 steps: treat/prevent hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, dehydration (ReSoMal, cautious), electrolytes, infection (antibiotics routinely), micronutrients, cautious feeding (F-75 → F-100) to avoid refeeding syndrome, catch-up growth, stimulation, follow-up).
Prevention
  • Exclusive breastfeeding to 6 months
  • Appropriate complementary feeding
  • Vitamin A
  • Food fortification
  • Rotavirus and measles vaccines
  • WASH (handwashing ↓ diarrhoea ~40%)
  • Deworming
  • Maternal nutrition
  • Cash transfers.

los.text: Discuss the cultural issues relating to the practice of female genital mutilation worldwide.
los.html:
FGM (WHO)
  • All procedures involving partial or total removal of external female genitalia or other injury for non-medical reasons.
  • Types: I (clitoridectomy), II (excision of clitoris + labia minora), III (infibulation: narrowing of vaginal opening), IV (other: pricking, piercing, cauterisation).
Prevalence
  • >200 million women/girls
  • Mainly Africa (Somalia, Guinea, Djibouti, Egypt, Sudan, Mali, Sierra Leone), Middle East, Asia
  • Diaspora communities in UK.
  • Usually performed in childhood (infancy to 15).
Cultural drivers
  • Social norm/convention (social acceptance, marriageability)
  • Rite of passage
  • Perceived purity, chastity, femininity
  • Controlling female sexuality
  • Perceived religious requirement (not required by any religion)
  • Family honour
  • Aesthetics
  • Maintained by older women
  • Increasingly "medicalised" in some countries.
Health consequences
  • Immediate: pain, haemorrhage, infection, urinary retention, shock, death.
  • Long-term: recurrent UTIs, dysmenorrhoea, keloid, cysts, sexual dysfunction, infertility, obstetric complications (prolonged labour, perineal tears, PPH, stillbirth), psychological trauma (PTSD).
UK law
  • Illegal (Female Genital Mutilation Act 2003), including taking a UK national/resident abroad for FGM
  • Max 14 years imprisonment.
  • Mandatory reporting duty: health professionals must report to police cases of FGM observed or disclosed in under-18s.
  • FGM Protection Orders.
  • Record in notes (FGM Information Sharing for at-risk girls).
Approach
  • Non-judgemental
  • Culturally sensitive
  • Use professional interpreter (not family)
  • Ask directly in at-risk groups (antenatal booking)
  • Safeguard daughters
  • Refer to specialist FGM clinic (deinfibulation)
  • Psychological support.
DebateCultural relativism vs universal human rights (WHO/UN: violation of rights of girls and women).

los.text: Recognise how diverse global factors affect health, well-being and health care delivery
sessions: Swansea Gambia Link: Challenges of practicing medicine and carrying out research in The Gambia
los.html:
Global factors
  • Poverty and economic inequality
  • Conflict and displacement
  • Climate change (heat, floods, food insecurity, vector-borne disease spread, migration)
  • Globalisation and trade (tobacco, ultra-processed food)
  • Urbanisation
  • Migration and human trafficking (exploitation, violence, untreated illness, mental health)
  • Pandemics and travel
  • Gender inequality
  • Governance and corruption
  • Health-worker migration ("brain drain").
Health systems in LMICs (e.g. The Gambia)
  • Limited workforce and specialists
  • Drug and equipment shortages
  • Out-of-pocket payments
  • Reliance on donors/NGOs
  • Infrastructure (electricity, water, transport)
  • Distance to facilities
  • Traditional healers
  • High burden of infection plus rising NCDs
  • Research challenges: ethics and consent (literacy, community consent), capacity, funding, equity in partnerships (e.g. MRC Unit The Gambia, Swansea–Gambia link).
Human trafficking
  • Recruitment by deception/coercion for sexual or labour exploitation, domestic servitude, criminal activity, organ harvesting
  • Signs in healthcare: accompanied by controlling person, no ID documents, inconsistent stories, untreated injuries, fearful
  • Refer via National Referral Mechanism, Modern Slavery Helpline.
Climate change
  • Called the greatest global health threat of the 21st century (Lancet Countdown)
  • NHS (and NHS Wales) net-zero targets
  • Healthcare itself contributes ~4–5% of emissions (inhalers, anaesthetic gases).
FrameworksSDGs (17 goals, 2030 agenda; SDG 3 = health, Universal Health Coverage), WHO, social determinants, "One Health" (human–animal–environment).

los.text: Describe factors affecting maternal health in the developing world
sessions: Maternal Health in the Developing World
los.html:
Maternal mortality
  • Death during pregnancy or within 42 days of its end from pregnancy-related causes.
  • ~260,000 deaths/year, ~95% in LMICs (~70% sub-Saharan Africa).
  • MMR (per 100,000 live births): >500 in some African countries vs ~10–13 in UK.
  • SDG 3.1 target: <70.
Direct causes
  • Haemorrhage (especially PPH, leading cause), hypertensive disorders (pre-eclampsia/eclampsia), sepsis, unsafe abortion, obstructed labour (→ uterine rupture, obstetric fistula), embolism.
  • Indirect: HIV, malaria, anaemia, heart disease.
"Three delays" model(Thaddeus & Maine)(1) deciding to seek care (knowledge, status of women, cost, cultural norms), (2) reaching care (distance, transport, roads), (3) receiving adequate care at facility (staff, blood, drugs, equipment).
Underlying factors
  • Poverty
  • Low female education and status
  • Adolescent pregnancy
  • High fertility/short birth intervals
  • Lack of family planning
  • FGM
  • Malnutrition/anaemia
  • HIV
  • Conflict
  • Weak health systems.
Interventions
  • Skilled birth attendance
  • Emergency obstetric care (antibiotics, uterotonics (oxytocin/misoprostol), magnesium sulfate, manual removal of placenta, assisted delivery, caesarean, blood transfusion)
  • Antenatal care (≥8 contacts WHO)
  • Family planning
  • Safe abortion services
  • Tranexamic acid for PPH (WOMAN trial)
  • Maternity waiting homes
  • Community health workers
  • Girls' education.

los.text: Recognise how diverse global factors affect health, well-being and health care delivery in UK
sessions: Q and A on asylum seekers
los.html:
UK diversity
  • ~18% of people in England and Wales belong to an ethnic minority group (2021 census)
  • Many languages
  • Migrants, refugees, Gypsy/Roma/Traveller communities, faith groups.
How global factors affect health in the UK
  • Migration (imported infections: TB, HIV, hepatitis B/C, malaria, parasites; under-immunisation)
  • Different disease patterns (South Asians: T2DM, CHD; Black African/Caribbean: hypertension, sickle cell, prostate cancer, stroke)
  • Health inequalities (Black women ~3× maternal death risk: MBRRACE-UK)
  • Language and health-literacy barriers
  • Racism and discrimination
  • Mistrust
  • Cultural beliefs about illness/treatment
  • Stigma (mental health, HIV)
  • Consanguinity (recessive disorders)
  • FGM
  • Trafficking/modern slavery.
Cultural competency
  • Awareness of own culture and biases, knowledge of other cultures (avoid stereotyping), skills to communicate across cultures
  • Cultural humility (lifelong learning, power balance).
Practice
  • Ask rather than assume (explanatory model: "What do you think caused this?")
  • Professional interpreters
  • Respect religious practices (fasting in Ramadan, dietary laws, modesty, blood products in Jehovah's Witnesses)
  • Involve family as the patient wishes
  • Culturally adapted health promotion
  • Address structural barriers.
WARD (Wales Asylum Seeker and Refugee Doctors)Supports refugee doctors to requalify (IELTS/OET, PLAB, GMC registration) and work in NHS Wales.

los.text: Describe the common medical problems faced by asylum seekers and refugees and explain the barriers they face in accessing healthcare services, including social, cultural, and logistical factors.
los.html:
Definitions
  • Asylum seeker = applied for protection, awaiting decision
  • Refugee = granted protection (1951 Refugee Convention: well-founded fear of persecution)
  • Refused asylum seekers
  • Undocumented migrants.
  • Wales aims to be a "Nation of Sanctuary".
Common medical problems
  • Mental health (PTSD, depression, anxiety, grief; torture and sexual violence; detention)
  • Infectious disease (TB, HIV, hepatitis B/C, parasites, scabies, malaria, incomplete immunisations)
  • Untreated chronic disease (diabetes, hypertension)
  • War injuries/chronic pain
  • Maternal health issues
  • FGM
  • Dental disease
  • Malnutrition/vitamin D deficiency
  • Children's developmental and educational needs
  • Risk of trafficking/exploitation.
Barriers to healthcare
  • Language/communication (lack of interpreters, using family/children as interpreters).
  • Social: poverty (~£49/week asylum support), unstable housing/frequent dispersal, isolation, no right to work.
  • Cultural: different health beliefs and expectations, stigma (mental health), gender preferences, mistrust of authorities.
  • Logistical/systemic: GP registration refused (wrongly: no proof of address/ID needed to register), transport costs, unfamiliar NHS system, digital access, NHS charging fears (secondary care charges for some migrants in England; in Wales asylum seekers and refused asylum seekers are exempt from charges), fear of data sharing with Home Office.
Good practice
  • Initial health assessment
  • Register with GP
  • Use professional interpreters (Language Line)
  • Trauma-informed care
  • Catch-up vaccinations
  • Screening (TB, BBV)
  • Safeguarding
  • Signpost to third sector (Welsh Refugee Council, British Red Cross, Freedom from Torture).

los.text: Recall international priorities in next decade
sessions: Q and A on asylum seekers
los.html:
Next-decade international priorities (2030 agenda)
  • Sustainable Development Goals, especially SDG 3 (good health and well-being): end preventable maternal, newborn and child deaths; end AIDS, TB, malaria and NTD epidemics; reduce NCD mortality by ⅓; mental health; road traffic deaths; Universal Health Coverage (UHC); reduce pollution deaths.
  • WHO "Triple Billion" targets: 1 billion more people benefiting from UHC, better protected from health emergencies, enjoying better health and well-being.
  • Pandemic preparedness (lessons from COVID-19; WHO Pandemic Agreement 2025; International Health Regulations).
  • Antimicrobial resistance.
  • Climate change and health (adaptation, net-zero health systems).
  • NCDs: tobacco control, hypertension, diabetes, cancer (cervical cancer elimination via HPV vaccination, screening and treatment: 90-70-90 targets).
  • Mental health, ageing populations, health workforce shortages, humanitarian crises/conflict, polio eradication, malaria elimination, nutrition (stunting), primary healthcare (Astana Declaration).
UK roleGlobal health security, research partnerships, aid (reduced recently), NHS workforce ethics (WHO Code on international recruitment of health personnel).

los.text: Describe a range of blood, tissue and GI parasites which infect humans, and their global impact.
los.html:
GroupParasiteDisease / featuresGlobal impact
Blood protozoaPlasmodiumMalaria~250 million cases, ~600,000 deaths/year (mostly African children)
Trypanosoma brucei (gambiense/rhodesiense; tsetse fly)African sleeping sickness: chancre, fever, lymphadenopathy (Winterbottom's sign) → CNS stage (sleep disturbance, coma)Declining; elimination targeted
Trypanosoma cruzi (triatomine "kissing" bug)Chagas disease: Romaña's sign → chronic cardiomyopathy, megaoesophagus/megacolonLatin America; migrants
BabesiaHaemolysisTicks
Tissue protozoaLeishmania (sandfly)Cutaneous (ulcer), visceral (kala-azar: fever, massive splenomegaly, pancytopenia)South Asia, East Africa, Brazil
ToxoplasmaCongenital, encephalitis in HIVWorldwide
GI protozoaGiardia, Entamoeba, CryptosporidiumDiarrhoea, dysentery, liver abscess
Helminths – blood/tissueSchistosoma (freshwater snails)S. mansoni: liver fibrosis/portal hypertension; S. haematobium: haematuria, bladder SCC~240 million infected
Filarial worms (Wuchereria: lymphatic filariasis/elephantiasis; Onchocerca: river blindness; Loa loa)NTDs
Echinococcus (hydatid cyst), Taenia solium (neurocysticercosis → epilepsy)
Helminths – GISoil-transmitted: Ascaris, hookworm (anaemia), Trichuris, Strongyloides~1.5 billion infected; childhood malnutrition, anaemia, impaired cognitionMass deworming
Global impact
  • Many are Neglected Tropical Diseases (NTDs): diseases of poverty causing chronic disability, stigma and economic loss
  • Control by mass drug administration, vector control, WASH.
Clues in returning travellers/migrantsEosinophilia (helminths), exposure history (freshwater swimming → schistosomiasis; barefoot → hookworm/Strongyloides).

los.text: Explain the pathogenesis, presentation, diagnosis, treatment and control of malaria
los.html:
Organism
  • Plasmodium falciparum (most severe; Africa)
  • P. vivax and P. ovale (hypnozoites in liver → relapse)
  • P. malariae
  • P. knowlesi (SE Asia; zoonotic, can be severe).
  • Transmitted by female Anopheles mosquito.
Life cycle/pathogenesis
  • Sporozoites
  • → liver (incubation ≥7 days, usually 1–4 weeks for falciparum; up to months/years for vivax/ovale)
  • → merozoites invade RBCs
  • → cyclical rupture
  • → fever paroxysms (tertian/quartan).
  • P. falciparum: infected RBCs express PfEMP1 → cytoadherence/sequestration in microvasculature → cerebral malaria, organ dysfunction
  • High parasitaemia
  • Haemolysis.
Presentation
  • Fever, rigors, sweats, headache, myalgia, vomiting, diarrhoea, cough (non-specific: "flu-like")
  • Splenomegaly, jaundice.
  • Severe falciparum: impaired consciousness/seizures (cerebral)
  • Parasitaemia >2% (UK threshold for severe)
  • Severe anaemia
  • Hypoglycaemia
  • Acidosis
  • AKI
  • ARDS/pulmonary oedema
  • Shock ("algid malaria")
  • DIC
  • Haemoglobinuria ("blackwater fever").
Diagnosis
  • Thick and thin blood films (thick: detection; thin: species and % parasitaemia) ×3 over 72 h if negative + rapid diagnostic test (antigen: HRP2/pLDH)
  • FBC (thrombocytopenia), U&E, LFT, glucose, lactate.
Treatment (UK)
  • Severe falciparum (or unable to take oral): IV artesunate → oral ACT when improved; ICU support; glucose monitoring.
  • Uncomplicated falciparum: artemisinin combination therapy (artemether–lumefantrine (Riamet) or Eurartesim) or atovaquone–proguanil (Malarone); admit initially.
  • Non-falciparum: ACT or chloroquine; primaquine (after checking G6PD) to eradicate hypnozoites (vivax/ovale).
Control/prevention
  • ABCD: Awareness of risk
  • Bite avoidance (DEET, long sleeves, insecticide-treated nets, indoor residual spraying)
  • Chemoprophylaxis (atovaquone–proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine; take before, during and after)
  • Prompt Diagnosis.
  • Globally: vector control, ACT, seasonal malaria chemoprevention, malaria vaccines (RTS,S, R21) for children in endemic Africa
  • Resistance (artemisinin partial resistance in SE Asia/East Africa).

los.text: Recognise the clinical issues with a returning traveller with fever
los.html:
Fever in a returning traveller from a malaria area = malaria until proven otherwise: same-day blood films/RDT, even if prophylaxis taken.
History
  • Where (country, rural/urban)
  • When (dates: incubation periods: <21 days excludes some, e.g. dengue <14 days)
  • Activities (freshwater, animal contact, insect/tick bites, sexual contact, food/water, healthcare abroad, safari, caves)
  • Prophylaxis and vaccines
  • Symptoms
  • Sick contacts.
Common causes
  • Malaria (most important)
  • Dengue (fever, headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia, rash, thrombocytopenia; warning signs → severe dengue/haemorrhage)
  • Enteric fever (typhoid: fever, relative bradycardia, abdominal pain, constipation then diarrhoea, rose spots; blood culture; ceftriaxone/azithromycin)
  • Travellers' diarrhoea
  • Respiratory infections (influenza, COVID-19, Legionella, MERS from Middle East)
  • UTI
  • Rickettsial infections (eschar, tick typhus: doxycycline)
  • Chikungunya
  • Zika
  • Hepatitis A/E
  • Amoebic liver abscess
  • Leptospirosis (freshwater, jaundice, AKI)
  • Schistosomiasis (Katayama fever)
  • HIV seroconversion
  • TB
  • Viral haemorrhagic fevers (Ebola, Lassa, CCHF: rare but high-consequence).
AssessmentABCDE, sepsis screen, isolate and contact infection team if VHF risk (travel to affected area within 21 days + fever: UKHSA VHF risk assessment algorithm before routine labs).
Investigations
  • Malaria films/RDT
  • FBC (thrombocytopenia: malaria/dengue; eosinophilia: helminths)
  • U&E
  • LFT
  • CRP
  • Blood cultures
  • Urine
  • CXR
  • Dengue NS1/serology
  • HIV test
  • Stool culture
  • Serology/PCR as indicated
  • Discuss with Rare and Imported Pathogens Laboratory / infectious diseases.
NotifiableMalaria, typhoid, VHF, etc.

los.text: To consolidate the learning objectives of the week and answer any residual questions.
los.html:
• High-yield summary of week 201:
    • Measuring health: DALYs = YLL + YLD; under-5 and maternal mortality; NCDs now dominate global deaths.
    • Child deaths: neonatal causes, pneumonia, diarrhoea, malaria; undernutrition contributes to ~45%. ORS + zinc; RUTF for SAM.
    • Maternal deaths: PPH, hypertension, sepsis, unsafe abortion; "three delays".
    • FGM: illegal in UK; mandatory police reporting for under-18s.
    • Asylum seekers/refugees: mental health, infections; barriers include language, cost fears, registration problems (no ID/address needed for GP registration).
    • Malaria: fever in returning traveller = films ×3; IV artesunate for severe falciparum; primaquine (G6PD check) for vivax/ovale.
    • Parasites: NTDs; eosinophilia clue; schistosomiasis → bladder cancer.
    • ICM: interpreters; ABCDE trauma (cABCDE).

los.text: Demonstrate the use of a translator or interpreter to obtain a comprehensive patient history, ensuring accuracy and understanding while maintaining patient dignity.
los.html:
Plan
  • Identify language and dialect needs in advance
  • Book a professional interpreter (face-to-face, video, or telephone e.g. Language Line)
  • Allow double time.
AvoidFamily members, children, friends or untrained staff as interpreters (confidentiality, accuracy, bias, safeguarding: may hide abuse/FGM/domestic violence).
Pre-brief interpreterPurpose of consultation, sensitive topics, confidentiality, ask for verbatim interpretation (first person), flag cultural issues.
Consultation
  • Seating in a triangle; speak directly to the patient (not the interpreter), maintain eye contact with patient, use first person ("How are you feeling?").
  • Short sentences, one question at a time, avoid jargon/idioms; pause for interpretation.
  • Check understanding (teach-back); allow patient questions.
  • Respect dignity and privacy: consider interpreter gender for intimate topics/examination; offer chaperone.
De-brief interpreter (emotional impact, cultural insights). Document interpreter name/ID, language, mode.
ConsentValid consent requires understanding through interpreter; written information in patient's language.

los.text: Conduct a structured patient history with a non-English-speaking patient using appropriate communication strategies, including using a translator or culturally sensitive techniques where necessary
los.html:
Structure
  • Still follow a full history (PC, HPC, PMH, DH + allergies, FH, SH, systems review, ICE) but adapt:
  • Introduce yourself and the interpreter's role; reassure about confidentiality.
  • Start with open questions, then focused closed questions; avoid leading and compound questions.
  • Use simple, concrete language; check meanings of symptoms that may be described differently across cultures (e.g. "heat", somatic expressions of distress; pain descriptors).
  • Culturally sensitive techniques: explore the patient's explanatory model ("What do you think is causing this? What worries you?"), traditional remedies/healers, religious practices (fasting, diet), family decision-making, gender preferences, preferred names/terms.
  • Ask about migration journey sensitively (trauma), housing, support, immigration status only if relevant, vaccination history, travel, screening.
  • Non-verbal: watch body language; be aware gestures can mean different things.
Close
  • Summarise (via interpreter)
  • Check understanding
  • Agree plan
  • Provide translated written information
  • Safety-netting in a way that works (how to access help, interpreters available free).
Telephone/video interpretingSpeakerphone, introduce everyone present, slow pace.

los.text: Perform a systematic ABCDE assessment in a clinical setting, prioritizing patient safety and identifying urgent issues that require immediate management.
los.html:
ApproachSafety first (danger), gloves/PPE, introduce, assess response (AVPU), call for help early. Primary survey: `<C>ABCDE` in trauma.
<C> Catastrophic haemorrhageDirect pressure, tourniquet, haemostatic dressings.
A – Airway with C-spine protection
  • Talking? noises (stridor, gurgling)
  • Look in mouth (blood, vomit, teeth)
  • Jaw thrust (not head tilt in trauma), suction, adjuncts (OPA/NPA; no NPA if base of skull fracture suspected)
  • Manual in-line stabilisation
  • Definitive airway if GCS ≤8.
B – Breathing
  • RR, sats, chest expansion, trachea, percussion, auscultation, chest wall (flail segment, wounds, surgical emphysema)
  • High-flow O₂ 15 L/min via non-rebreathe mask.
  • Treat immediately: tension pneumothorax (needle/finger decompression), open pneumothorax (vented dressing), massive haemothorax (chest drain).
C – Circulation
  • HR, BP, CRT, skin colour/temperature, sources of bleeding: "on the floor and four more" (chest, abdomen, pelvis, long bones)
  • 2 large-bore cannulae, bloods incl.
  • Crossmatch, VBG lactate, pelvic binder, splint femur
  • Tranexamic acid
  • Blood products.
D – DisabilityGCS/AVPU, pupils, glucose, limb movement (spinal injury).
E – Exposure/environmentFull exposure, log roll (back, spine), prevent hypothermia, temperature.
Reassess after every intervention; then secondary survey (top-to-toe, AMPLE history: Allergies, Medications, Past history, Last meal, Events). Handover with SBAR/ATMIST.

los.text: Describe the principles of trauma resuscitation, including key interventions, and explain their rationale for use in stabilizing patients in critical care situations.
los.html:
PrinciplesTreat greatest threat to life first (<C>ABCDE), "golden hour", team-based approach with team leader, reassess frequently, prevent secondary injury.
Key interventions and rationale
  • Haemorrhage control (pressure, tourniquets, pelvic binder, splints, surgery/IR): haemorrhage is the leading preventable cause of trauma death.
  • Damage control resuscitation: permissive hypotension (SBP ~80–90 or palpable radial pulse until bleeding controlled; avoids dislodging clot and dilution; not in head injury: maintain cerebral perfusion), early blood products (major haemorrhage protocol: RBC + FFP + platelets ~1:1:1, cryoprecipitate), minimise crystalloids (dilutional coagulopathy), tranexamic acid within 3 h (CRASH-2: ↓ mortality), avoid lethal triad (hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy: warm patient and fluids).
  • Airway protection with C-spine immobilisation (manual in-line stabilisation; collars less routine now).
  • Oxygenation and ventilation; decompress tension pneumothorax (2nd ICS MCL or 4th/5th ICS mid-axillary).
  • Damage control surgery: stop bleeding and contamination, then ICU, definitive repair later.
  • Head injury: avoid hypoxia and hypotension, CT head, neurosurgery.
  • Imaging: CT ("trauma CT" head to pelvis), eFAST ultrasound, CXR/pelvic X-ray in resus.
  • Analgesia, tetanus, antibiotics for open fractures.
Trauma systems
  • South Wales Trauma Network: Major Trauma Centre at University Hospital of Wales, Cardiff
  • Morriston (Swansea) is a trauma unit and the regional burns and plastics centre
  • Pre-hospital EMRTS (Wales Air Ambulance).
